title: Probability
prerequisites: Ability to work with fractions and percentages.
Idea of counting favourable cases out of total cases.
Familiarity with dice, coins and playing cards.

topics.title: Empirical Probability
topics.quick_summary: Empirical or experimental probability is the ratio of the number of times an event occurs to the total number of trials, and it approaches the theoretical value as trials increase.
topics.real_life: A weather forecast of 70% rain comes from records of past days with similar conditions — empirical probability at work.

detailed.definition: The empirical probability of an event E is P(E) = (number of trials in which E happened) / (total number of trials). A trial is one performance of an experiment.
detailed.key_idea: Empirical probability is based on actual observation and can change with each new set of trials, whereas theoretical probability is computed from the structure of the experiment and does not.
detailed.working_principle: The law of large numbers guarantees that as the number of trials grows, empirical probability settles closer and closer to the theoretical value.
applications: Insurance premiums are computed from empirical probabilities of claims.
Quality control estimates defect rates by sampling.
Medical trials estimate the probability of a treatment succeeding.

points: P(E) = 0 means an impossible event; P(E) = 1 means a certain event.
The sum of the probabilities of all elementary outcomes is 1.
mistakes: Reporting a probability greater than 1 or negative.
Dividing by the number of favourable cases instead of the total.
Assuming a small number of trials gives a reliable estimate.
topics.memory_hook: 'Favourable over Total — and the answer can never leave the range 0 to 1.'
topics.advanced: The gambler's fallacy — believing a coin is 'due' to land heads after several tails — comes from confusing the law of large numbers with a short-run correction. Independent trials have no memory whatsoever.
